lede: Some responses happen before you have decided anything. A spinal reflex runs from a receptor, through three neurones inside the spinal cord, out to a muscle — the shortest route there is, which is exactly why it is fast enough to protect you.
can: Name the three neurones and describe the pathway in order.
Say what a synapse is and how an impulse crosses it.
Explain why extra synapses slow a response down.

md: Touch something hot and your hand is already moving before you have felt the pain. The message never went to your brain; it went into your spinal cord, crossed to a second neurone and came straight back out to the muscle.

prompt: The neurone that carries the impulse from the receptor towards the spinal cord is the ______ neurone.
explain: Sensory — it carries the message from the sense. Motor carries it out to the muscle, and the association neurone links the two inside the cord.

md: **Stage by stage.** A **stimulus** (a change, such as heat) is detected by a **receptor**, which produces **nerve impulses**. The impulse travels along the **sensory neurone** into the **spinal cord**. There it crosses a **synapse** to the **association neurone**, then another synapse to the **motor neurone**, which carries it out to the **effector** — a **muscle or gland** — which produces the **response**.

alt: Six boxes in a chain joined by arrows: stimulus, receptor, sensory neurone, association neurone, motor neurone, and effector leading to response, with the two synapses marked underneath between the three neurones.

title: CCEA's word is 'association'
md: Many textbooks and videos call the middle neurone the **relay** neurone. CCEA's specification and its glossary both call it the **association** neurone, and that is the word the mark schemes list. Write **association neurone**; if you have learnt 'relay', write both the first time and then use CCEA's word.

title: GCSE Biology - The Nervous System | Reflex Arcs Explained (2027/28 exams)
why: The reflex arc drawn stage by stage, with the synapses shown rather than glossed over. Note that it uses 'relay neurone' — CCEA's word is association. Watch it, then answer the question underneath.

prompt: In a spinal reflex arc, which neurone lies between the sensory and the motor neurone?
explain: The association neurone, inside the spinal cord. Some books call it the relay neurone; CCEA's schemes want 'association'.

md: A **synapse** is the **gap between two neurones**. The impulse cannot cross it directly: the first neurone releases a **chemical**, which **diffuses across the gap** and starts a **new impulse** in the next neurone. Diffusion is slower than an impulse travelling along a neurone, so **every synapse adds a delay**. A spinal reflex arc has exactly **two** — one on each side of the association neurone — and that is the smallest number the pathway can have, which is part of why a reflex is so fast.

prompt: What crosses the gap at a synapse?
explain: A chemical diffuses across and starts a new impulse in the next neurone.

title: Why the neurones do not simply join up
md: Only the first neurone at a synapse can release the chemical, and only the second can detect it. That makes every junction a **one-way valve**: an impulse can never run backwards out of a motor neurone.

title: March 2026 B1 Higher Q6(c) and Summer 2024 B1 Foundation Q4
md: In March 2026, asked what more synapses would do to the speed of a response, **most candidates said it would be slower but fewer gave a correct explanation**. The explanation is the chemical: at each gap a chemical has to be released and diffuse across, and diffusion takes longer than conduction along a neurone. In Summer 2024 candidates **named the neurones correctly** but **fewer answered the question about a synapse**, which suggests the gap is learnt as a word rather than as a mechanism.

prompt: How many synapses are there in a spinal reflex arc with three neurones?
explain: 2 — one between the sensory and association neurones, and one between the association and motor neurones. Three neurones always give two joins.

prompt: Why does adding more synapses to a pathway make the response slower?
options: At each synapse a chemical has to diffuse across the gap, which takes time
The impulse gets weaker each time it crosses a gap
Each synapse sends the impulse backwards for a moment
answer: At each synapse a chemical has to diffuse across the gap, which takes time
explain: Diffusion across the gap is the slow step. That is the explanation March 2026's candidates could not give.

task: Trigger an impulse and watch it run the length of the neurone. Then write one sentence explaining why a pathway with two synapses in it takes longer than the same length of a single, unbroken neurone.

text: Why the brain is not in the picture

md: A **spinal** reflex is co-ordinated in the **spinal cord**, not the brain. The impulse goes in, crosses to the association neurone and comes straight back out — the shortest route there is. That is why a reflex takes a fraction of a second: an impulse travelling 1.5 m at about 50 m/s takes 1.5 ÷ 50 = 0.03 s. You do become aware of it, because impulses also travel up to the brain — but the muscle has already moved by then.

prompt: An impulse travels 1.5 m at 50 m/s. How long does it take, in seconds?
explain: time = distance ÷ speed = 1.5 ÷ 50 = 0.03 s. Keep the units consistent — metres with metres per second gives seconds.

prompt: Which structure co-ordinates a spinal reflex?
explain: The spinal cord. Keeping the brain out of the loop is what makes the response fast enough to be protective.
